```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(shinyOAuth)
```

An app may need to read a calendar and call a contacts API after the same user
signs in. Those APIs can require different access tokens. Token targets let
you name each API, declare the permissions it needs, and ask a connection for the
right token without building a separate login flow for each API.

Your provider must support this: shinyOAuth supports RFC 8707 resource indicators
and Microsoft's API-specific scopes. Check your provider's registration and
consent requirements before enabling targets. The provider can still refuse an
API or decline to issue a refresh token.

For separate accounts or independent logins, use
[Multiple authorizations](multiple-authorizations.html) instead. For basic login
setup, start with [Usage](usage.html).

## Configure two APIs

This example uses a provider that supports RFC 8707. A resource identifies
an API to the login provider; scopes name the permissions for that API.
A resource identifier is not necessarily the address your R code calls.
`resource_bases` lists the HTTP addresses a connection may use.

Replace the example URLs and permissions with your provider's settings. For
Microsoft, use the [Microsoft example](#microsoft-example) below.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Use this mode only after confirming RFC 8707 support with your provider.
provider <- oauth_provider(
  "workplace", "https://login.example/authorize", "https://login.example/token",
  token_target_mode = "rfc8707",
  token_auth_style = "body",
  userinfo_required = FALSE
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTH_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example/callback",
  scopes = c("calendar.read", "calendar.write", "contacts.read"),
  token_targets = list(
    calendar = list(
      resource = "https://calendar.example/",
      scopes = c("calendar.read", "calendar.write"),
      required_scopes = "calendar.read",
      resource_ids = "calendar_api"
    ),
    contacts = list(
      resource = "https://contacts.example/",
      scopes = "contacts.read",
      resource_ids = "contacts_api"
    )
  ),
  default_token_target = "calendar",
  resource_bases = c(
    calendar_api = "https://calendar.example/v1",
    contacts_api = "https://contacts.example/v1"
  )
)
```

`default_token_target` selects the API used when a connection method omits
`target`. It is required for several targets; a single target is selected
automatically. `resource_ids` connects each target to the named HTTP API addresses
in `resource_bases`. You can omit HTTP addresses if you only export tokens to
another package.

## Choose a token when making a call

Obtain the connection from either module's `connection()` method. Pass `target`
to choose an API; the app does not need to keep its own token cache.
`existing_contacts_sdk()` below stands for the client constructor from your
chosen contacts package; replace it with that package's actual function.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth", client,
    reauth_after_seconds = 60 * 60 # Example: choose the app's login lifetime.
  )
  # Alternatively: auth <- oauth_connections_server("auth", manager)
  # and select auth$connection(connection_id), or auth$connection() when unique.

  contacts <- shiny::reactive({
    connection <- shiny::req(auth$connection())
    token <- connection$access_token("contacts.read", target = "contacts")
    existing_contacts_sdk(access_token = token)$list_contacts()
  })

  output$can_edit_calendar <- shiny::renderText({
    connection <- shiny::req(auth$connection())
    connection$has_scopes("calendar.write", target = "calendar")
  })

  shiny::observeEvent(input$save_event, {
    connection <- shiny::req(auth$connection())
    connection$request(
      "calendar_api", "events", method = "POST",
      required_scopes = "calendar.write", target = "calendar", refresh = TRUE,
      configure = function(req) httr2::req_body_json(req, list(title = input$title))
    )
  })
}
```

`$access_token()` obtains or refreshes the selected API's token when needed.
`$has_scopes()` checks permissions already recorded for that API and does not
fetch a token. It can therefore return `FALSE` before the first acquisition.
`$targets()` lists API names, status and granted permissions without exposing
tokens.

`$request(refresh = TRUE)` refreshes before sending, but does not replay a failed
API call. Run writes from explicit user actions and let the user decide whether
to try again.

Choose a login lifetime when enabling targets. Without `reauth_after_seconds`,
`auth$authenticated` can remain true for the rest of the Shiny session even when
all API tokens have expired. The example sets a one-hour local login limit.
`indefinite_session = TRUE` ignores that limit. Connection methods still require
a valid token and the permissions for the selected API.

## Microsoft example

```{r, eval=FALSE}
provider <- oauth_provider_microsoft(
  tenant = Sys.getenv("MICROSOFT_TENANT_ID"),
  userinfo_required = FALSE
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider, Sys.getenv("OAUTH_CLIENT_ID"), Sys.getenv("OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example/callback",
  scopes = c(
    "openid", "offline_access",
    "https://graph.microsoft.com/Calendars.Read",
    "api://your-contacts-api/Contacts.Read"
  ),
  token_targets = list(
    calendar = list(
      resource = "https://graph.microsoft.com",
      scopes = "https://graph.microsoft.com/Calendars.Read"
    ),
    contacts = list(
      resource = "api://your-contacts-api",
      scopes = "api://your-contacts-api/Contacts.Read"
    )
  ),
  default_token_target = "calendar"
)
```

`oauth_provider_microsoft()` selects Microsoft's API-specific scope handling.
Use the fully qualified permission names from your registration. Setting
`userinfo_required = FALSE` avoids requesting a Graph profile with a token
intended for another API; identity-token validation stays enabled.

This example exports bearer tokens to another package. Add `resource_bases` and
target `resource_ids` if you also want to use `$request()`.

## Refresh and sign in again

For RFC 8707 providers, you can reduce one API's permissions with, for example,
`connection$refresh(scopes = "calendar.read", target = "calendar")`. The other
API keeps its own permissions; requesting its token does not restore removed
calendar permissions. Required scopes must remain present.

`auth$reauthorize()` starts a replacement login with the reduced permissions.
With a connection manager, pass the connection ID. Once replacement starts,
cancelling or failing login does not restore the old connection. Use an ordinary
new login when you intend to request the client's original permissions again.
Microsoft's restrictions on narrowing are described below.

## Advanced: provider support and declaration limits

Targets share one local login and refresh credential, while keeping separate
access tokens and permission limits. Providers must explicitly enable
`token_target_mode = "rfc8707"` or `"microsoft"`; discovery does not infer support.
Targets require `userinfo_required = FALSE` and cannot be combined with the
client's `resource` argument or SMART configuration. Put resource declarations
in `token_targets`, not in provider extra parameters. The older
`oauth_connection(client, token_reactive)` wrapper does not support targets;
use a module's `connection()` method.

Up to 16 targets are supported. The complete login has a limit of 128 distinct
scope names and 8192 scope bytes, excluding separating spaces. These totals
include OIDC scopes and actual Microsoft permissions, including `.default`
expansions. Declarations may use vectors or space-delimited strings. Callback
and encrypted-state size limits still apply; very large declarations may need
larger state limits.

In RFC 8707 mode, authorization requests carry all declared resources and scopes.
Token requests select one resource and its scopes. The provider decides which
permissions apply to each resource; the authorization request does not pair
individual scopes with resources. See [RFC 8707](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8707.html).

### Identity and refresh-consent scopes

For OIDC providers, declare `openid`, `profile`, `email`, `address`, `phone` and
`offline_access` at client level rather than in an API's scope list. RFC 8707
mode recognizes these as OIDC scopes when the provider uses OIDC or client scopes
include `openid`. Otherwise they are ordinary API scopes and belong in targets.
Microsoft recognizes only `openid`, `profile`, `email` and `offline_access` as
its OIDC scopes.

Client-level `required_scopes` may contain OIDC scopes only, except
`offline_access`. Request `offline_access` in client `scopes` if you need refresh
consent; it is not a required access-token permission and must not appear in
client or target `required_scopes`. Its presence in a scope list does not prove
that a refresh token was issued.

When explicitly narrowing a target, retain any OIDC scopes it still needs,
for example `scopes = c("calendar.read", "openid")`. Optional identity scopes
are not added back by refresh. Refresh consent is tracked separately because
providers may issue a refresh token without reporting `offline_access` in access
token scopes. Explicitly removing that scope removes it from the target's later
reauthorization request. Reauthorization combines the retained target limits,
so an OIDC scope kept by another target may still be requested.

An OIDC replacement always requests `openid` for its new identity check, including
for the default target. Removed API permissions and optional OIDC scopes stay
removed; secondary targets keep their own limits.

`connection$identity()` returns selected claims from the last validated identity.
With targets it can remain available after the primary API token expires or no
longer includes `openid`. It does not establish fresh authentication or current
API access; use the selected target's request or token methods for those checks.

## Advanced: Microsoft permissions and consent

Microsoft can return previously consented permissions beyond the ones your app
requested for a particular operation. Connection permission checks still enforce
the app's retained limits, while `$targets()` reports the actual provider grant.
An exported bearer token carries that full grant; shinyOAuth cannot restrict
what an SDK does with it.

For this reason, explicit Microsoft API narrowing through `$refresh(scopes = ...)`
is unsupported and fails with reason `unsupported_scope_narrowing` before sending
a request. The existing login stays usable. Use a separate app registration or
change provider consent if the token itself must have fewer API permissions.

### Resource identifiers and scope names

Microsoft resource identifiers may be absolute URIs or GUIDs. For example,
`499b84ac-1321-427f-aa17-267ca6975798/.default` requests static permissions for
that GUID resource. Resource identifiers match exactly, including a trailing
slash; adding `/.default` to a slash-terminated resource produces a double slash.
API scopes must name a permission after the exact resource prefix and slash.

Distinct resources must not have overlapping prefixes. For example,
`https://api.example` and `https://api.example/reports` make `reports/read`
ambiguous. Targets may share the exact same resource with separate limits.

Microsoft permission names are compared without ASCII case sensitivity;
resource identifiers remain exact. Ordinary OAuth scopes remain case-sensitive.
Microsoft token responses must include `scope`. Short permission names are
qualified with the selected resource before connection checks, including checks
on custom introspection results. Public `introspect_token()` results keep the raw
provider scope string.

### Static permissions and unusual short names

Use `resource/.default` as a target's sole API scope for static consent, and
include it in client `scopes`. Do not mix it with explicit API scope declarations.
`required_scopes` must name actual API permissions; `.default` requests consent
and is not evidence that any individual permission was granted. Use the exact
lowercase `.default` spelling.

For optional short permissions containing `:` or `/`, a target can declare
`scope_aliases = c("items/read", "read:items")`. They identify response names that
shinyOAuth may recognize; they do not request permissions, make them required,
or expand the app's limits. Unknown punctuated short names must be returned in
fully qualified form. Names containing `://` or a declared resource prefix are
always treated as qualified names.

If a partial grant leaves a target with no API permissions, acquisition fails
with `insufficient_scope` rather than making an OIDC-only request for a different
API. A replacement login with an API-empty default target is rejected before
ending the current login. Start a new login to request the original permissions.

See Microsoft's [authorization code flow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/v2-oauth2-auth-code-flow),
[scope and consent guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/scopes-oidc),
and [refresh token guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity-platform/refresh-tokens).

## Advanced: concurrent refreshes and failures

Several target acquisitions may need the same refresh token. Async calls
coordinate their work and use the latest refreshed credential. A synchronous
call reports `refresh_pending` while async work owns it. A rejected request for
one API can leave the other tokens usable, but a failure that might have consumed
the shared refresh credential can make the entire login require reauthorization.

With `indefinite_session = TRUE`, the single module may retain usable cached API
tokens after such a failure, but retires the shared refresh credential. It cannot
refresh expired tokens or acquire a new target without a new login. A connection
manager has no indefinite-session exception. Separate managed logins sharing
the same refresh credential also follow the manager's shared-credential rules.

`token_stale` describes the primary token; refreshing a secondary API token does
not clear it. `authenticated` describes the retained local login. Connection
methods check the selected API token and permissions before use. Logout,
replacement and session end invalidate old connections and late results.

The modules check replacement state size before ending a current login. If this
local preparation fails, the connection remains usable. Once replacement starts,
a later failure or cancellation does not restore it.

Logout removes local access before best-effort remote revocation. Target tokens
are included in that cleanup, but the provider may be unavailable or reject a
revocation request.

### Request customization and background work

`$request(refresh = TRUE)` is synchronous. It validates the destination and the
prepared request before refreshing, runs `configure` once, and checks permission
again before sending. It disables ordinary HTTP retries for that call. DPoP nonce
handling remains available, but no API error triggers a new login or replay of
the business request. `$access_token()` exports bearer tokens only; use
`$request()` for DPoP or mTLS-bound tokens.

For SDK callbacks, background tasks and checks before displaying results, see
[External integrations](external-integrations.html).
